idiom_name: immutable interval value with explicit bound kinds plus containment and overlap operations
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one immutable value holding two endpoints, each tagged as closed, open or unbounded, with named factories (closed, closedOpen, atLeast, atMost, all, empty) as the only way to build it, and a constructor that rejects an upper endpoint preceding the lower one. The query surface is includes(value), includes(range) or overlaps(range), plus the interval-to-interval results intersection, span and gap/abut; operations that are only defined for connected ranges should say so and fail fast rather than returning a meaningless value. Where the standard library already encodes bound kinds (RangeBounds/Bound in Rust, Range/ClosedRange/partial ranges in Swift, Range in Ruby and Kotlin), collapse the classic two-field class into those types and add only the operations they lack - usually overlap and intersection. Where the domain is discrete, decide explicitly whether to canonicalise, because structural equality will otherwise disagree with set equality.
code_sketch:
r  = interval.closed_open(start, end)    # [start, end)
assert r.includes(now)
assert not r.overlaps(other)

open_ended = interval.at_least(start)   # [start, +inf)
empty      = interval.empty()

# partial operations: test first, or fail fast
if r.overlaps(other):
    both = r.intersection(other)
pitfalls: Encoding "unbounded" with sentinel endpoints (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31, -inf as a magic string) leaks into arithmetic and comparisons, and the sentinel eventually becomes a real value.
Building the interval from raw endpoints without validating their order, so every later comparison inherits a reversed interval.
Treating structural equality as set equality: over a discrete domain two different representations can denote the same values, and empty intervals are unequal unless canonicalised.
Answering overlap with an inequality that only handles half-open bounds, so closed intervals that share exactly one endpoint are reported as disjoint (or vice versa.),

Wrong move: Treat PostgreSQL's default range constructor as a closed business interval -> the upper endpoint is excluded and equality at that boundary changes membership -> instead choose and document the bound convention, using an explicit bound specification when the domain requires another one.

Wrong move: Use a range value as an iterable of every contained value -> arbitrary comparable domains have no enumeration and large discrete spans can be impractical -> instead use a discrete-domain iterator such as Guava ContiguousSet or a range container when that is the actual requirement.

Wrong move: Call intersection without checking connectivity or overlap -> disconnected ranges cannot yield one contiguous interval, while merely touching ranges may yield an empty boundary range and APIs may reject disconnected inputs -> instead test isConnected/overlaps first and model disjoint results as a multirange or interval set.
